name: 酒と肴 なかむら (Sake to Sakana Nakamura)

claims.text: As a traditional Japanese izakaya, dishes rely on soy sauce and dashi-based seasonings, which typically contain wheat; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

name: 茶論 奈良町店 (Salon Naramachi)

claims.text: Seasonal Japanese wagashi and matcha are the core offering; many such sweets are rice- and bean-based, giving a starting point for plant-based diners who confirm ingredients with staff.

name: 晴朗邸 勝手口 (Seiroutei Katteguchi)

claims.text: Home-cooking dishes such as meat-and-tofu stew and sautéed greens with fried tofu rely on Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, mirin) that typically contain wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is indicated.
Cooking is built on homemade dashi, which at a fish-and-meat izakaya is typically fish/kombu based, so vegetable dishes are unlikely to be vegan.
All dishes are made by hand using the owners' own dashi, described as gentle and homemade — a small kitchen where you can ask the couple directly about ingredients.

name: 重乃井 奈良店 (Shigenoi Nara-ten)

claims.text: The shop's core product is hand-made wheat udon kneaded and cut on-site, so flour is present throughout the kitchen and there is no gluten-free preparation.

The dipping dashi is based on kombu, dried shiitake, and three types of bonito; as a traditional Japanese tsuyu it is expected to contain soy sauce (and thus wheat), and is in any case served with wheat noodles.
The dashi contains three kinds of bonito (fish), so the broth is not vegan, and lunch sides include fish/egg items such as inari-zushi and chirashi-zushi.
Soups, simmered vegetable dishes and pickles use standard Japanese seasonings; soy sauce in Japan typically contains wheat and no wheat-free soy sauce is documented here.
The menu offers fish, Yamato beef and Yamato chicken alongside the vegetable courses, and soups/hot pots are likely fish-dashi based; no separate vegan preparation is documented.
The cuisine is built around Yamato vegetables with a dedicated vegetable lunch course, making it easier than most restaurants to eat largely plant-based if you confirm the dashi and seasonings.
Tempura is battered in wheat flour and fried in a shared kitchen; no dedicated fryer or gluten-free preparation is documented, so cross-contamination should be assumed.
Dishes such as saikyo-grilled salmon and sashimi are served with soy sauce and miso, which in standard Japanese kitchens contain wheat.
The kitchen handles fish, shellfish and meat throughout, and broths use fish dashi, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable in the seasonal small-dish format.

name: そば処 吟松 奈良町店 (Soba-dokoro Ginsho Naramachi-ten)

claims.text: The soba is nihachi (二八), an 80% buckwheat / 20% wheat blend, so the noodles inherently contain wheat; udon (pure wheat) is also cooked here, and tempura is wheat-batter fried in shared oil.
Soba is served with a bonito-dashi tsuyu/broth; standard Japanese soba tsuyu is soy-sauce based, which normally contains wheat. No wheat-free sauce is documented.
The broth and dipping sauce use bonito (fish) dashi, and signature dishes are tempura and tendon, so dishes are prepared in a fish- and animal-using kitchen with no documented vegan separation.

name: そば処 季のせ (Soba-dokoro Kinose)

claims.text: The kitchen prepares both 100% buckwheat soba and wheat-containing two-eight (nihachi) soba plus tempura, so even the jūwari soba is highly likely to share equipment and water with wheat products.
Soba is served with a Kanto-style broth/dipping sauce based on soy sauce, which contains wheat.
Broth is fish-dashi based and the menu includes egg and tempura dishes; no vegan-dedicated preparation is documented.
Diners may eat the soba with a pinch of salt instead of sauce, which avoids the wheat-containing broth (though the noodles themselves are not certified gluten-free).
